title: People With Type 2 Diabetes Face Up to 25 Times Higher Risk of Severe Dengue, Review Warns
excerpt: A comprehensive review highlights that diabetic patients who contract dengue for the first time face dramatically worse outcomes, a finding with urgent relevance as India enters peak monsoon season.
body:
• A comprehensive medical review warns that people with type 2 diabetes who contract dengue for the first time face up to 24 times higher odds of progressing to severe disease
  • Diabetic dengue patients show lower platelet counts, higher rates of dengue hemorrhagic fever, and elevated mortality compared to non-diabetic patients
  • India is home to over 100 million people with diabetes and reports hundreds of thousands of dengue cases annually, making the overlap a major public health concern
  • Experts advise diabetic individuals to take aggressive mosquito prevention measures during monsoon season, especially those travelling to dengue-endemic areas

A Dangerous Overlap

People with type 2 diabetes face a dramatically elevated risk of developing severe dengue if they contract the mosquito-borne virus, according to a comprehensive medical review that health experts say carries urgent implications for India as the monsoon season intensifies.

The review, drawing on multiple peer-reviewed studies including research published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases and the International Journal of Infectious Diseases, found that diabetic patients contracting dengue for the first time — without prior immunity — face odds ratios as high as 24.3 for progressing to severe disease forms including dengue hemorrhagic fever and dengue shock syndrome.

A large retrospective study of 644 dengue patients at Kaohsiung Medical University Hospital found that diabetic patients had significantly higher rates of dengue hemorrhagic fever and dengue shock syndrome (56.9 percent versus 33.9 percent in non-diabetic patients) and more severe thrombocytopenia — dangerously low platelet counts — during the first three days of hospitalisation.

Why Diabetes Makes Dengue Deadlier

Researchers point to several mechanisms. High blood sugar levels impair immune function, making it harder for the body to fight the dengue virus effectively. Diabetes also causes chronic low-grade inflammation and vascular dysfunction, which can compound the vascular leakage that makes dengue hemorrhagic fever so dangerous.

A study from a major South Indian teaching hospital identified diabetes as an independent predictor of severe dengue, with an adjusted odds ratio of 2.12 — meaning diabetic patients were more than twice as likely to develop severe disease even after accounting for age, gender, and other factors.

"Diabetes was the predominant comorbidity documented among severe dengue cases, closely followed by hypertension. These two conditions are components of metabolic syndrome, the ultimate consequences of which can encompass cardiovascular diseases and potential fatality if not managed effectively."

— Peer-reviewed dengue research published in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases

The India Factor

The findings are particularly alarming for India, which sits at the intersection of two epidemics. The country is home to more than 100 million people with diabetes — the second-highest number globally after China — and reports hundreds of thousands of dengue cases each year, with the true burden likely far higher due to underreporting.

As monsoon rains spread across the country, creating ideal breeding conditions for the Aedes aegypti mosquito that transmits dengue, the convergence of these two health challenges presents a significant public health risk. The India Meteorological Department has forecast heavy rainfall across more than 60 percent of the country through late July.

What NRIs Travelling to India Should Know

For members of the Indian diaspora planning monsoon-season visits, experts recommend that those with diabetes take aggressive mosquito prevention measures. This includes using DEET-based repellents, wearing long-sleeved clothing, ensuring accommodation has proper screening or air conditioning, and avoiding outdoor exposure during dawn and dusk hours when Aedes mosquitoes are most active.

Diabetic travellers who develop fever, body aches, or rash within two weeks of visiting a dengue-endemic area should seek medical attention immediately and inform their physician of their diabetes status, as early intervention is critical for preventing progression to severe disease.
